new: According to the IPCC (Summary for Policymakers, statement B.7.3), the larger the overshoot, the more net negative CO2 emissions would be needed to return to 1.5°C by 2100, and transitioning towards net zero CO2 emissions faster and reducing non-CO2 emissions such as methane more rapidly would limit peak warming levels and reduce the requirement for net negative CO2 emissions, thereby reducing feasibility and sustainability concerns and social and environmental risks associated with CDR deployment at large scales (high confidence) [2].

According to the IPCC, modelled pathways that limit warming to 1.5°C (>50%) with no or limited overshoot reach median values of cumulative net negative emissions of 220 GtCO2 by 2100, while pathways that return warming to 1.5°C (>50%) after high overshoot reach median values of 360 GtCO2 (high confidence) [2].

The IPCC finds, with high confidence, that afforestation, reforestation, improved forest management, agroforestry and soil carbon sequestration are currently the only widely practiced CDR methods [2].

The 2018 review also finds that a substantial gap exists between the upscaling and rapid diffusion of negative emission technologies implied in scenarios and progress in actual innovation and deployment, that if they are required at the scales currently discussed, the resulting urgency of implementation is currently neither reflected in science nor policy, and that they face severe barriers to implementation and are only weakly incentivized so far [5].

The 2018 review cautions that if near-term emission reductions follow the pathways suggested by current NDCs, there will be a fundamental dependence on negative emissions by 2030 in 2°C scenarios, with such delayed-action scenarios showing no available scenarios without negative emission technologies, large-scale deployment of 250−920 GtCO2 throughout the 21st century, and rapid upscaling between 2030 and 2050 (0.2−0.7 GtCO2 per year) to 3−14 GtCO2 [5].
The review cautions that its carbon budget figure is not fixed: 'Estimation of carbon budget depends on temperature data used, and various methodological assumptions' [5].

The review's authors also single out, in their view, three issues in need of future ethical analysis: that NETs might create a moral hazard against mitigation, that "an implicit policy bet on NETs that are unproven at scale may lock in worse climate-related harms if they failed to deliver," and that "the sheer scale of NETs deployment observed in mitigation scenarios is staggeringly hubristic" [5].
